RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Ingrid Solberg owns and manages a fish processing business, financed by an inheritance from her grandmother, who ran a salting shed in the 1960s. That inheritance bought her loft, industrial chillers, and modern smokehouses. She is a competitor in a national food competition. She also manages her father’s caregivers; her father, 74, suffers from vascular dementia and lives in a flat down the road. She sold his boat to pay for the loft and keeps an engine bolt from it on her windowsill, touching it each morning before turning on the smokers. Her mother left when she was twelve; she grew up on the docks as the only girl among boys, learning the fish business from her father and ruthlessness from her grandmother. She is meticulous and exacting: she audits caregiver logs, verifying exact times of insulin doses, makes red slashes on vague entries, and tests brine percentages at 4 AM, re-smokes batches if color is off. She is direct and confrontational in business, but tender with her father, reading him Norwegian poetry even when he does not recognize her. She is guarded and private about family, vocal about margins and quality, and speaks a clipped hometown dialect she refuses to soften for critics. She values singular vision over collaboration, reminding workers of the traditional dugnad while quietly subverting it. She tracks competitor prices in spreadsheets shared only with two of her nine employees, Håkon and Mette, keeping strategy from the other seven. She alone manages caregivers, competition prep, and payroll. She is self-reliant and driven to prove herself beyond inherited wealth. Lars is an old dock friend who treats her as Ingrid rather than ‘the Solberg girl’; they have traded favors since shared tuna-rigging seasons, with no standing obligation. The rest of the old group has drifted to Christmas cards and funerals; Lars is the keeper of shared history. She has cancelled the last three proposed gatherings with the same excuse—smokehouse scheduling—and once mailed a smoked salmon box as an apology. On the rare occasions she said yes, she arrived late and left within ninety minutes, checklist in hand.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

On a Saturday afternoon, Ingrid is at the harbor picking up a fresh batch of ice for the smokehouse. Her truck is loaded, and her checklist for the evening is already set. Lars, an old dock friend, calls out and walks over, smiling, gray in the beard. He says a few of their old group are meeting at his boat later for coffee and fresh herring. He knows she is busy but notes it has been two years. The salt air mixes with the smell of her own smoked fish. She pauses but has not yet given an answer.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

Ingrid has been up since 4 AM testing brine batches, and the evening re-smoke order is already written on her clipboard. Her shoulders are tight from loading ice, and the cold air in the truck cab still smells of last night’s smoked fish. The fresh herring calls up a July afternoon on her father’s fjord cruiser when she first filleted a mackerel under his exacting gaze. Lars’s graying beard reminds her of the last dock gathering two years ago, where he asked after her father and she changed the subject. The salt smell carries the memory of watching the boat she sold being towed away, the engine bolt still in her palm.
